unit.title: Putting it all together
unit.description: Combining signals, top-down analysis, testing rules and knowing what works

u23l1.title: Confluence: signals that confirm each other

steps.title: What confluence is
steps.body:
A single signal is a weak clue. When **different pieces** point to the same thing, the idea carries more weight:

• **Trend:** highs and lows, 200 SMA.
• **Level:** support, resistance or a key average.
• **Signal:** a confirmed reversal candle or a breakout on volume.
• **Volume:** more people behind the move.

steps.title: The redundant-indicator trap
steps.body:
RSI, stochastic and CCI measure almost the same thing: momentum. Three of them aren’t three confirmations: they’re one, repeated.

Better to use a few tools of **different types**: trend (averages), momentum (RSI or MACD), volatility (Bollinger, ATR) and volume.

steps.title: And even so, a plan
steps.body: With confluence, the idea is better, not certain. Before you enter: where the stop is, where the target is and how much you’re risking. If the target isn’t at least 2 times the stop distance away, it’s not worth it.
steps.key: Look for agreement between different pieces, not for more indicators.
steps.tip: Ten indicators aren’t ten opinions: often they’re the same one, repeated.

steps.title: Top-down
steps.body:
Analysing several timeframes stops you trading against the current:

1. **Higher (weekly):** what’s the long-term trend?
2. **Intermediate (daily):** is there a pullback or a pattern?
3. **Lower (hourly):** where do the entry and the stop go?

It’s Alexander Elder’s triple screen method.

steps.title: The method in 7 steps
steps.body:
1. Weekly: trend and 200 SMA.
2. Structure of highs and lows.
3. Levels.
4. Current situation: near a level or in a pattern?
5. Signal on the daily chart.
6. Indicators as a filter.
7. Plan: entry, stop, target and risk.

steps.title: When they don’t agree
steps.body: If the weekly is bearish and the daily gives a buy signal, that signal goes against the current: many traders ignore it or cut the size. Timeframes that don’t agree are information too.
steps.key: First the direction on the higher timeframe; then the timing on the lower one.
steps.tip: Before you look at the five-minute candle, check where the weekly one is.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
A **backtest** tests a specific rule («I buy when the price closes above the 200 SMA and sell when it closes below») on past data, to see what would have happened.

The rule is written **before** looking at the results, with entries, exits, stops and costs.

steps.title: The traps
steps.body:
• **Overfitting** (*data snooping*): you test so many variants that one comes out well by chance.
• **Look-ahead bias:** using data that weren’t known yet at that moment.
• **Survivorship bias:** testing only on companies that are still around today.
• **Forgetting costs:** commissions, *spread* and taxes.

steps.title: How to keep it honest
steps.body: Split the data: design the rule with one part (**in-sample**) and test it just once on another part you haven’t looked at (**out-of-sample**). If it only works on the first part, it was luck.
steps.key: A backtest tells you what would have happened, not what will happen.
steps.tip: Torture the data long enough and they’ll confess to anything.

steps.title: What the evidence supports
steps.body:
• **Momentum and trend following:** trends of 3–12 months have tended to persist in shares, bonds, currencies and commodities (Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993; Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen, 2012; Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen, with data going back to 1880).
• Between 30 and 40 % of professionals surveyed consider it important in the short term.

steps.title: What doesn’t pass the tests
steps.body:
• Park and Irwin (2007) reviewed 95 modern studies: 56 positive, 20 negative and 19 mixed… but most had problems of method (data snooping, poorly estimated risk and costs), and the most recent ones find little or no edge in shares.
• Candlesticks: no proven value after costs.
• Fibonacci, Elliott waves, Gann: no rigorous evidence.

steps.title: Why learn it anyway
steps.body: To set entries, exits and stops logically, understand what others are doing and spot people selling smoke and mirrors. A small edge with good risk management can be enough; a big edge without risk management ends in ruin.
steps.key: Trend and momentum have evidence behind them; many other ideas don’t pass the tests.
steps.tip: Technical analysis doesn’t tell you the future: it helps you decide where you’re wrong and how much it costs you.

u23l1-1.prompt: You already have the RSI on screen. Which pieces would add different information? Select all that apply.
u23l1-1.explanation: The stochastic and the CCI measure momentum, just like the RSI: they don’t add a new opinion.

u23l1-2.prompt: What counts as confluence in favour of a possible buy? Select all that apply.
options: High volume on the reversal candle
The pattern appearing in a viral video
u23l1-2.explanation: Trend, level, signal and volume are pieces of the chart. A video’s popularity or your fondness for the company aren’t.

u23l1-3.explanation: Trend, momentum and volume measure different things.

u23l1-4.prompt: You enter at €50 with the stop at €48. What’s the minimum price the target should be at for a 2 to 1 reward-to-risk ratio?

u23l1-5.prompt: Does it count in favour of a buy or not?
options: A breakout on double the average volume
A bounce off support that has held three times
u23l1-5.explanation: Different pieces of the chart count; repeated ones and other people’s opinions don’t.

u23l1-6.prompt: Look for trend, levels and candles on this chart. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u23l1-6.explanation: Even with several signals in your favour, the outcome over 10 sessions is uncertain. Confluence improves the odds; the stop protects you when they fail.

u23l1-7.prompt: Another chart, same method. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u23l1-7.explanation: Always apply the same steps: that way you’ll know whether your method adds anything or whether you just remember the hits.

u23l1-8.prompt: You have confluence and enter at the last price. Place the stop where the idea stops being valid.
u23l1-8.explanation: Below the recent low: if the price loses it, the pieces that made you enter no longer hold.

u23l1-9.prompt: Pablo has 9 indicators on screen: 6 say «buy» and 3 say «sell». What’s wrong?
options: Many of them probably measure the same thing and the vote means nothing
He has a crystal-clear signal: 6 to 3
u23l1-9.explanation: Confluence comes from different pieces, not from counting indicators.
feedback: Adding more just multiplies the chance coincidences.
Exactly: better a few tools of different types than a parliament of oscillators.
If several measure the same thing, that 6 to 3 may be 1 to 1, repeated.

u23l1-10.prompt: Three momentum oscillators that agree are three independent confirmations.
u23l1-10.explanation: They measure almost the same thing: it’s a single opinion, repeated.

u23l2-1.prompt: Put the top-down analysis in order.
options: Pullback or pattern on the daily
Entry and stop on the hourly chart
u23l2-1.explanation: From the general to the specific: direction, timing and entry.

u23l2-2.prompt: Put the 7 steps of the method in order.
options: Plan: entry, stop, target and risk
u23l2-2.explanation: The plan always comes last and is never skipped.

u23l2-3.prompt: First screen: the long-term trend. What do you see? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u23l2-3.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows: against this backdrop, a buy signal on the daily would go against the current.

u23l2-4.prompt: Weekly: lower highs and lower lows, and the price below the 200 SMA. Daily: a beautiful hammer appears. What’s the sensible thing to do?
options: Treat it as a counter-trend signal: either ignore it or trade it smaller and with a stop
u23l2-4.explanation: The higher timeframe sets the context; the lower one shouldn’t just contradict it.
feedback: A hammer isn’t a sell signal, and a long-term portfolio doesn’t depend on one candle.
Exactly: when the timeframes don’t agree, the signal carries less weight.
The hammer goes against the long-term trend: in that context it’s a weak signal.

options: Weekly bearish and buy signal on the daily
Weekly bearish and downside breakout on the daily
Weekly bullish and sell signal on 5 minutes
Weekly bullish and buy signal on the daily
u23l2-5.explanation: Aligned when the signal goes in the direction of the higher timeframe.

u23l2-6.prompt: First the big picture: 30 daily candles. Up or down over the next 10?
u23l2-6.explanation: Not even looking at several timeframes lets you guess the short term. The method helps you avoid trading against the current and know where the stop goes.

u23l2-7.prompt: Another asset. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u23l2-7.explanation: An orderly method cuts silly mistakes; it doesn’t remove uncertainty.

u23l2-8.prompt: In the triple screen method, what is the lower timeframe for?
options: Fine-tuning the entry and the stop
u23l2-8.explanation: The higher one gives the direction; the intermediate one, the timing; the lower one, the entry and the stop.

u23l2-9.prompt: Quick: who came up with the triple screen method?
u23l2-9.explanation: Alexander Elder, in Trading for a Living.

options: The weekly first, because it sets the direction; the 15-minute chart only fine-tunes the timing
The 15-minute one, because it’s the most recent
u23l2-10.explanation: The higher timeframe rules; the lower one fine-tunes.
feedback: That’s it! Top-down: direction, timing and entry.
They help you organise the decision and set the stop logically, even if they don’t predict.
The most recent isn’t the most important: on 15 minutes, noise rules.
lines: On the 15-minute chart I can see a massive rally 🚀
But on the weekly it’s in free fall 📉
Which one should I listen to?

u23l3-1.prompt: You test 100 rules that don’t actually work. If each one has a 5 % chance of looking good by luck, how many do you expect to «work»?
u23l3-1.explanation: 100 × 0.05 = 5. If you only show those 5, it’ll look like you’ve discovered something.

u23l3-2.prompt: A rule makes an average gross profit of 0.10 % per trade. Each trade costs 0.15 % in commission and spread. What’s the net result per trade?
u23l3-2.explanation: 0.10 − 0.15 = −0.05 %. With costs, the «edge» turns into a loss.

u23l3-3.prompt: A rule is right 40 % of the time and makes €300 when it’s right; the other 60 % of the time it loses €100. How much does it make on average per trade?
u23l3-3.explanation: 0.4 × 300 − 0.6 × 100 = 120 − 60 = €60. You can be wrong more often than right and still make money, if the gains are bigger than the losses.

u23l3-4.prompt: Match each trap with its example.
u23l3-4.explanation: Each trap inflates past results in a different way.
right: Testing only on the companies in the index today
Using the day’s close to buy at that same day’s open
Testing 500 combinations of averages and keeping the best one

u23l3-5.prompt: Marta tests 300 variants of a rule on data from 2015 to 2020 and keeps the one that made 40 % a year. What should she do before trusting it?
options: Look for a variant that makes 60 %
Test it just once on data she hasn’t used (for example, from 2021 to 2024) and with costs
Use it right away with all her money
u23l3-5.explanation: The out-of-sample test is what separates a rule from a fluke.
feedback: Testing more variants makes the problem worse: more flukes disguised as discoveries.
Exactly: if it deflates out of sample, it was overfitting.
With 300 variants, the best one may be pure luck. Without an out-of-sample test, she knows nothing.

u23l3-6.prompt: Bruno runs a backtest from the year 2000 with the 35 companies that make up the IBEX 35 today. The results look spectacular. What’s the problem?
options: That the year 2000 is too recent
Survivorship bias: it leaves out the ones that dropped out of the index or disappeared
u23l3-6.explanation: Choosing the data with today’s information is cheating without meaning to.
feedback: The period isn’t the main problem: picking the companies by looking at the present is.
They’re real, but they’re the ones that survived and grew. The ones that fell or left the index aren’t there.
Exactly: testing on today’s winners inflates past results.

u23l3-7.prompt: What does testing a rule «out of sample» mean?
options: Testing it on data that weren’t used to design it
Testing it only on the best years
u23l3-7.explanation: It’s the acid test: new data the rule hasn’t «seen».

u23l3-8.prompt: What did Sullivan, Timmermann and White (1999) do with moving-average rules?
options: They corrected for data-snooping bias, and the results weakened considerably
u23l3-8.explanation: Much of what looked like an edge was partly luck.

u23l3-9.prompt: A good backtest guarantees the rule will work in the future.
u23l3-9.explanation: It tells you what would have happened with that data. The future may be different.

options: Can you send me the rule?
How many variants did you test, and what happens with costs and with data you haven’t used?
When are you going all in?
u23l3-10.explanation: Variants tested, costs and out-of-sample data: the three questions for any backtest.
feedback: Before copying it, it’s worth checking whether that 80 % is real or an overfitting mirage.
Nice! Those questions knock down most spectacular backtests.
First you’d need to see whether it survives costs and new data.
lines: I’ve run a backtest and my rule makes 80 % a year 🤑

u23l4-1.prompt: Momentum is one of the most studied anomalies in finance, with data covering more than a century.
u23l4-1.explanation: Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen studied it with data going back to 1880, although exploiting it after costs is hard.

u23l4-2.prompt: According to Park and Irwin, the positive studies on technical analysis have no problems of method.
u23l4-2.explanation: They warn that most of them do: data snooping and difficulty estimating risk and costs.

u23l4-3.prompt: There’s rigorous evidence that Elliott waves predict the market.
u23l4-3.explanation: Neither Elliott waves, nor Fibonacci, nor Gann have rigorous evidence behind them.

u23l4-4.prompt: Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen studied trend following with data going back to 1880.
u23l4-4.explanation: More than a century of data, with long drawdowns along the way.

u23l4-5.prompt: Which technical analysis idea has the most academic support?
u23l4-5.explanation: It’s the exception with the most evidence, across many markets and over a long time.

u23l4-6.prompt: What does the evidence say about each tool?
u23l4-6.explanation: Trend and momentum are the parts with the most support; the rest, at best, helps organise decisions.
right: No rigorous evidence or no value after costs

u23l4-7.prompt: A Telegram channel promises a technical system that «wins 95 % of trades, with no losses». What do you think, given what you’ve learnt?
options: That I’ll try it with a little money, just in case
That it’s an impossible promise: the evidence points to small edges, if any, and always with losses
That someone has finally cracked it
u23l4-7.explanation: Promises of near-perfect accuracy clash with all the available evidence.
feedback: Trying it «with a little» still means handing money and data to someone promising the impossible.
Exactly: even what has evidence behind it, like momentum, suffers long drawdowns.
No serious study finds anything like it; 95 % with no losses is a classic sign of hype or a scam.

u23l4-8.prompt: Ana uses technical analysis like this: she marks where she’s wrong (stop), risks 1 % per trade and doesn’t chase «the perfect pattern». What do you think?
options: That she uses it sensibly: as a risk management tool, not a crystal ball
That she should risk 20 % per trade to make it worthwhile
That she’s wasting her time: without the perfect pattern you can’t win
u23l4-8.explanation: Used with humility and risk management, technical analysis is a useful tool.
feedback: Exactly: the value lies in deciding where you’re wrong and how much it costs you.
With 20 % per trade, a few losses in a row would knock her out of the game.
The perfect pattern doesn’t exist; looking for it is the trap.

u23l4-9.prompt: What does any technical tool need to be of any use?
u23l4-9.explanation: A big edge without risk management ends in ruin; a small one with good management can be enough.

u23l4-10.prompt: One last test of humility: 30 real candles, no name. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u23l4-10.explanation: After the whole section, the honest conclusion is the same: nobody reliably gets the short term right. What you do control is how much you risk.

u23l4-11.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes, always: with practice you get everything right
Some ideas have evidence behind them (trend, momentum), many don’t, and nothing works without risk management
u23l4-11.explanation: Neither magic nor hype: some pieces work some of the time, and risk management works all the time.
feedback: That’s not what the evidence says: many rules stop working on new data.
Not that either: trend and momentum have more than a century of evidence, even if they’re hard to exploit.
Exactly! A useful tool, not a crystal ball.
lines: So… does technical analysis work or not? 🤔
